content: The evidence was summarized and critically appraised using the Cochrane methodology for randomized controlled trials and observational studies. Evidence summaries were prepared following the GRADE approach to evaluate the overall quality of the evidence. The GRADE framework considers factors such as study design, limitations in study conduct and analysis, consistency of results across studies, directness of evidence in relation to the populations, interventions, and settings, and the precision of the effect estimates. Both systematic reviews and GRADE evidence profiles for critical outcomes were utilized in drafting the guideline. The draft recommendations were discussed by the WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guidelines Development and the WHO guideline development group during meetings held in Geneva, Switzerland, in March 2011 and June 2014. Decision-making procedures were established at the start of these meetings, including rules for agreement and documentation. At least two-thirds of the guideline development group needed to be present for initial discussions on evidence and proposed recommendations. Members of the group anonymously recorded their views on the direction and strength of the recommendations, as well as their opinions on the intervention's effects, evidence quality, values, preferences, and cost implications in different settings. The WHO Secretariat collected and summarized the voting results, and if unanimous consensus was not achieved, further deliberations and a second round of online voting were conducted. If consensus was still not reached, a two-thirds majority vote was required for approval. Divergent opinions could be documented in the guideline. Voting records were retained by WHO for up to five years. Although unanimous consensus was not achieved, over 80% of the group members deemed each recommendation strong. WHO staff and external technical experts involved in evidence collection and grading did not participate in the decision-making process. Two co-chairs with expertise in group processes and evidence interpretation were nominated and approved at the start of the consultation. WHO Secretariat members were available to guide the meeting process but did not vote or have veto power. Regarding the management of competing interests, all experts participating in WHO meetings were required to declare any relevant interests before their involvement. Declarations of interest were reviewed by the responsible technical officer and relevant departments before finalizing the group composition. Participants submitted declarations of interest and their CVs before each meeting and verbally declared potential conflicts at the start of the meetings. The management of conflicts of interest adhered strictly to WHO guidelines. Specific cases of declared interests were addressed individually. For example, Dr. Beverly-Ann Biggs declared funding received by her institution for research on iron and folic acid supplementation in pregnancy. It was agreed that she could fully participate in deliberations and decision-making. Dr. Luz Maria De-Regil disclosed her employment with an organization focused on improving micronutrient status, primarily funded by the Canadian government. She participated in deliberations but recused herself from voting on iron supplementation recommendations. Dr. Lynette Neufeld declared her employer's past funding for iron supplementation research and disclosed her prior role commissioning related research. She participated in discussions but abstained from voting on iron supplementation recommendations. Dr. Héctor Bourges Rodríguez declared his role as chair of a non-profit organization funded by a food company but was allowed full participation as the company did not manufacture products related to anemia or iron supplementation. External experts also declared their interests but did not participate in deliberations or decision-making. The WHO Secretariat will continue monitoring research developments in oral iron supplementation for infants and children in malaria-endemic and non-endemic settings, particularly for areas where evidence quality is low. If an update to the guideline is warranted, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will coordinate the process following WHO's formal procedures. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, a search for new evidence will be conducted to ensure its validity.
